lesson.title: Containers from Zero, part 4: files that outlive the container
lesson.description: Give hello-app a visit counter, watch the count vanish with the container, then keep it with a named volume and share it with a bind mount. Learn to tell which mount a container uses, and who owns the files it writes.
lesson.tested: Kept hello-app 1.2 visit counts in a named volume and a bind mount on Engine 29.10.1, 25 Nov 2026
lesson.rule: Put data you keep in a named volume, use a bind mount when you need the files on the host, and check with docker inspect which one you have.

boards.title: Where /data/visits.txt ends up
boards.hint: the program writes /data either way; the mount decides where the bytes go

rows.name: no mount
rows.role: The container's writable layer, on top of the read-only image layers.
rows.where: deleted; the next container starts at visit 1

rows.name: named volume
rows.role: `hello-data`, a directory Docker manages under `/var/lib/docker/volumes/`. Do not edit it there; mount it into a container.

rows.name: bind mount
rows.role: A host folder you chose, such as `/home/ubuntu/hello/data`. Host and container edit the same files.

rows.name: anonymous volume
rows.role: A volume with a random name, for example from an image that declares `VOLUME`. Not shared automatically.
rows.where: kept, unless the container ran with `--rm`

boards.note: A mount hides whatever the image had at that path. An empty named volume is first filled with the image's files at that path.

rows.name: volume, long
rows.where: a typo in the name makes a new, empty volume

rows.name: bind, long
rows.where: refuses a missing path: `bind source path does not exist`

rows.name: bind, short
rows.where: creates a missing path as a root-owned directory

rows.name: your user
rows.where: otherwise files the app creates belong to root

steps.note: Safety: the lab deletes the volume `hello-data` and the `data` and `missing` folders it creates in `hello`. Rename them if yours already exist. Undo with `docker rm -f hello`, `docker volume rm hello-data`, `rm -rf data`, `rmdir missing`.

sections.title: Recall
sections.hint: Answer from memory, then check the lesson.

exercises.q: What happens to files a container writes to its writable layer when you run `docker rm`?
exercises.a: They are deleted with the container. Docker's storage overview: data written to the container layer does not persist when the container is destroyed.

exercises.q: Name the two mount types from the lesson and say who decides where the files live.
exercises.a: A named volume: Docker manages the directory. A bind mount: you choose the host path, and host and container share the same files.

exercises.q: Why should you not edit files under `/var/lib/docker/volumes/` directly?
exercises.a: Docker's docs call direct access to volume data unsupported, undefined behavior that may break the volume or its data. Mount the volume into a container instead.

exercises.q: How do `--mount` and `-v` differ when the host path of a bind mount does not exist?
exercises.a: `--mount` stops with `bind source path does not exist`. `-v` creates the path, always as a directory, owned by root.

exercises.q: Which command removes a named volume, and when does it refuse?
exercises.a: `docker volume rm hello-data`. It refuses with `volume is in use` while any container, running or stopped, still uses it.

exercises.q: Run hello-app:1.2 with no mount, `curl` twice, `docker rm -f hello`, run it again and `curl`. What count do you get, and why?
exercises.a: visit 1 again. The count file was in the first container's writable layer, which `docker rm` deleted.

exercises.q: Repeat with `--mount type=volume,src=hello-data,dst=/data`. What count does the new container give?
exercises.a: visit 3. The file was in the volume `hello-data`, which removing the container left alone.

exercises.q: Run the `docker inspect --format` command from the lesson on the running container. What does each field tell you?
exercises.a: `volume hello-data /var/lib/docker/volumes/hello-data/_data -> /data`: the type, the volume name, where Docker keeps it, and the path inside the container.

exercises.q: Bind-mount a `data` folder, write 41 into `data/visits.txt` from the host, then `curl`. What do you get, and what is in the file afterwards?
exercises.a: visit 42, and the file contains 42. Host and container read and write the same file.

exercises.q: Let the container create `data/visits.txt`, then run `ls -l data` and `echo 5 > data/visits.txt`. What happens, and how do you avoid it?
exercises.a: The file is owned by `root root` and the write fails with `Permission denied`. Run the container with `--user "$(id -u):$(id -g)"` so it writes as your user.

sections.title: Predict the outcome
sections.hint: Write your prediction first. Then check the answer key.

exercises.q: You type `--mount type=volume,src=helo-data,dst=/data` by mistake. What count do you see, and why?
exercises.a: visit 1. Docker created a new, empty volume named `helo-data`; your count is still in `hello-data`.

exercises.q: You run `-v data:/data` from the `hello` folder, expecting your `data` folder. What does Docker mount?
exercises.a: A named volume called `data`. Without a path, `-v` reads the first part as a volume name. Use `"$PWD"/data:/data`.

exercises.q: You add `readonly` to the bind mount and `curl` the app. What does `curl` print, and where is the reason?
exercises.a: `curl: (52) Empty reply from server`. `docker logs` shows `OSError: [Errno 30] Read-only file system: '/data/visits.txt'`.

exercises.q: You run `docker volume rm hello-data` while a stopped container still uses it. What happens?
exercises.a: Docker refuses with `volume is in use` and lists the container ID. Remove the container first.
